newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's CAE Cargo to acquire four Embraer 120.
newsitem.headline: France's CAE Cargo to acquire four Embraer 120.

text.p: French cargo charter airline, CAE Cargo International, said it planned to acquire four Embraer Brasilia EMB 120s over the next year or so as part of a fleet renewal programme.

CAE managing director, Stephane Brun, told Reuters in an interview that the company expects a 1997 turnover of 40 million francs on the basis of existing signed contracts. It had a 1996 turnover of 16 million francs,he added.
CAE's current fleet comprises four Fairchild Metroliners and two Fokker 27-500Fs.

"The first of the EMB 120s is scheduled for delivery within the next three months with the second probably following in the early autumn and the remaining two during 1998. We also plan a gradual phase-out of the Metroliners,"
He added: "The EMB120s can carry up around three-and-a-half tonnes of cargo compared to around two tonnes for the Metroliners, he said.

The second-hand planes are being acquired from France's Aerospatiale via its AI(R) leasing unit. However, the precise terms and conditons of the deal are still under discussion, Brun said. The aircraft were previously leased to another French airline, Air Littoral.

Around one-third of CAE's activity is in regular cargo charters. Its main client is the French express distribution group, Jet Services, for whom it operates weeknight freighter flights between Liege and Paris-Charles de Gaulle and Kassel (Germany) and CDG using 6.5 tonne capacity Fokker 27-500Fs.

Another third of the airline's business is accounted for by ad hoc cargo charter flights, especially for the automotive parts industry where its major customer is forwarding group, Gefco,a 100 percent subsidiary of French car manufacturer, Peugeot.
The remaining third of CAE's activity is taken up by the transport of dangerous goods - chemicals, explosives, armements, radio-active matter and other contaminated materials.

"This is a very under-developed market in France with the main air cargo carriers absent despite the fact that for some categories of dangerous goods air transport is the sole option. According to French civil aviation authority estimates, in 1996, we accounted for over 80 percent of flights designated to be transporting dangerous goods."
Paris/CDG-based CAE handled 144 dangerous goods shipments last year, a 200 percent rise on 1995, Brun added.
The majority of these shipments were carried on intra-European routes but long-haul destinations, via stopovers, have included Rio in Brazil and Santiago in Chile.

"We have developed an expertise in this sector with each of our staff, whatever their grade, trained in handling dangerous goods while we also have strong links with our customers' technical staff to ensure a global, coherent service. --Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542-7706 Fax+5017
